questions.question_text:
Verify by differentiation and substitution that $Q=32+9e^{kt}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-32)$, where $k\ne0$.
Which calculation gives the correct verification?

options.why: Introduces a negative sign in both the derivative and the substitution; the exponential term in $Q$ is positive.

options.text: $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=9e^{kt}$ and $k(Q-32)=9e^{kt}$, so both sides agree for every nonzero $k$.
options.why: Omits the factor $k$ from both expressions; these expressions agree with the required sides only when $k=1$.
Differentiates the constant $32$ as $32k$ and fails to subtract $32$ when evaluating the right-hand side.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=32+9e^{kt}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=9ke^{kt}$
Also $Q-32=9e^{kt}$, so $k(Q-32)=9ke^{kt}$.
Both sides equal $9ke^{kt}$, so the function satisfies the differential equation.

questions.question_text:
A quantity is modelled by $Q=240+Ae^{kt}$, and $Q=95$ when $t=0$.
What is the value of $A$?

options.why: Takes $A$ to be the initial value of $Q$, but $A$ is the initial difference $Q(0)-P$.
Finds the size of the gap but drops the sign; here $Q$ starts below $240$.
Adds $95$ and $240$ instead of substituting $t=0$ and solving $95=240+A$.

questions.question_text:
A temperature is modelled by $T=12+48e^{kt}$, and $T=30$ when $t=6$.
What is $k$ in exact form?

options.why: Inverts the ratio when taking logarithms, giving a positive $k$ for a falling temperature.
Uses the temperatures themselves as the ratio $\frac{30}{12}$ instead of the difference from $12$.
Divides $30$ rather than $30-12$ by $48$, forgetting to subtract the fixed value first.

questions.question_text:
Verify by differentiation and substitution that $Q=24+16e^{-0.5t}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.5(Q-24)$.
Which calculation gives the correct verification?

options.why: Drops the negative sign from both the exponent's derivative and the coefficient on the right-hand side.
Uses a factor of $-1$ instead of $-0.5$ in both calculations.
Treats the derivative as $-0.5Q$ and forgets to subtract $24$ on the right-hand side.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=24+16e^{-0.5t}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=16(-0.5)e^{-0.5t}=-8e^{-0.5t}$
Also $Q-24=16e^{-0.5t}$, so $-0.5(Q-24)=-8e^{-0.5t}$.
Both sides agree, so the function satisfies the differential equation.

questions.question_text: Which description matches the graph of $Q=50-35e^{-0.4t}$ for $t\ge0$?

options.text: It starts at $Q=15$ and increases towards the horizontal asymptote $Q=50$.
It starts at $Q=85$ and decreases towards the horizontal asymptote $Q=50$.
options.why: Changes the subtraction to addition when calculating the initial value, giving $50+35=85$.

options.text: It starts at $Q=15$ and decreases without bound.
options.why: Treats the exponent as positive, so the subtracted term grows instead of tending to zero.

options.text: It starts at $Q=50$ and decreases towards the horizontal asymptote $Q=15$.
options.why: Swaps the fixed value $50$ with the initial value $50-35=15$.

questions.solution_text:
$Q(0)=50-35e^0=15$.
As $t\to\infty$, $35e^{-0.4t}\to0$, so $Q\to50$ from below.
The graph starts at $(0,15)$ and increases towards the horizontal asymptote $Q=50$.

questions.question_text: Which description matches the graph of $Q=65-40e^{-0.25t}$ for $t\ge 0$?

options.text: It starts at $Q=25$ and increases towards the asymptote $Q=65$.
It starts at $Q=65$ and decreases towards the asymptote $Q=25$.
options.why: Swaps the fixed value with the starting value, reading $65$ as $Q(0)$.

options.text: It starts at $Q=25$ and increases without bound.
options.why: Ignores that $e^{-0.25t}\to 0$, which caps the curve at $Q=65$.

options.text: It starts at $Q=40$ and increases towards the asymptote $Q=65$.
options.why: Uses the magnitude $|A|=40$ as the starting value instead of computing $Q(0)=65-40$.

questions.solution_text:
$Q(0)=65-40e^{0}$
$=25$
As $t\to\infty$, $40e^{-0.25t}\to 0$, so $Q\to 65$ from below and $Q=65$ is a horizontal asymptote.

questions.question_text:
Verify by differentiation and substitution that $Q=20-7e^{-2t}$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-2(Q-20)$.
Which calculation gives the correct verification?

options.why: Drops the negative sign in the term $-7e^{-2t}$ in both calculations.
Omits the factor $2$ from both the derivative and the multiplication on the right-hand side.
Uses $-2Q$ for the derivative and forgets to subtract $20$ when evaluating the right-hand side.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=20-7e^{-2t}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=(-7)(-2)e^{-2t}=14e^{-2t}$
Also $Q-20=-7e^{-2t}$, so $-2(Q-20)=14e^{-2t}$.
Both sides agree, so the function satisfies the differential equation.

questions.question_text:
A quantity is modelled by $Q=30+Ae^{kt}$, with $Q=90$ when $t=0$ and $Q=66$ when $t=4$.
What is the value of $Q$ when $t=8$?

options.why: Assumes $Q$ falls by a constant $24$ every $4$ units of time instead of by a constant factor.
Substitutes $90$ for $60$ only in the final calculation while retaining the correctly calculated factor $e^{4k}=0.6$, giving $30+90(0.6)^2=62.4$.
Multiplies $Q=66$ by the factor $0.6$ without first subtracting the fixed value $30$.
